title: Neuroblastoma in Children
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Neuroblastoma is an embryonal tumour of the sympathetic nervous system, most common in children under 5. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues, imaging, and pathology, with staging guiding treatment and prognosis.

sections.p: Neuroblastoma arises from primitive neural crest cells of the sympathetic chain, adrenal medulla or paraspinal ganglia. It presents as a solid mass, often with metastases to bone marrow, bone, and liver.
b: Tumour of sympathetic nervous system
Most common solid tumour in infants <2 y
Diagnosed by tissue histology showing small round blue cells with rosettes

t.b: Detects a solid adrenal or retroperitoneal mass; guides need for further imaging
Defines tumour size, local invasion and distant spread; essential for staging
Shows catecholamine‑avid disease; if unavailable, use bone scan or PET‑CT
Elevated in >90 % of cases; a positive result supports diagnosis
Provides histology and MYCN status; required for definitive diagnosis

sections.p: The International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) system uses imaging‑defined risk factors, age, histology, MYCN amplification and DNA ploidy to assign low, intermediate or high risk.
b: Age <18 months generally favourable
MYCN amplification = high‑risk
Stage 4 = distant metastases

t.b: Answers the question of disease extent; guides therapy intensity

sections.p: Neuroblastoma is sporadic; a small proportion are familial due to ALK or PHOX2B mutations. No infectious aetiology, but co‑existing conditions common in low‑resource settings (e.g., malaria‑related anaemia) may mask presentation.
b: Sporadic somatic mutation (most common)
Familial ALK or PHOX2B mutation
Rare association with congenital syndromes (e.g., Hirschsprung disease)

sections.p: Presentation varies with tumour site and stage. Common clues are an abdominal mass, constitutional symptoms, and paraneoplastic signs.
b: Palpable, non‑tender abdominal mass in infants
Weight loss, fever, irritability
Opsoclonus‑myoclonus (dancing eyes‑dancing feet) syndrome
Hypertension (catecholamine excess)
VIP‑secreting tumours cause watery diarrhoea

sections.p: Prioritise bedside‑available tests; when advanced imaging is lacking, use clinical staging and urine catecholamines.
b: Full blood count – look for anaemia or marrow infiltration
Serum ferritin – may be raised in metastatic disease

t.b: Confirms catecholamine production; a normal result does not exclude disease

t.a: Bone marrow aspirate (if anaemia or bone pain)
t.b: Detects marrow metastasis; essential for stage 4 classification
Screens for lung metastases when CT unavailable

sections.p: Rapid tumour growth, spinal cord compression, and severe hypertension demand urgent action.
b: Progressive abdominal distension with respiratory compromise
Neurological deficit from spinal involvement
Uncontrolled hypertension or cardiac failure

sections.p: Treatment follows risk stratification. Low‑risk disease may be observed or resected; high‑risk disease needs multimodal therapy.
b: Surgical excision of primary tumour when feasible
Induction chemotherapy (e.g., cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine) for high‑risk
Myeloablative therapy with autologous stem‑cell rescue for very high‑risk
Retinoic acid differentiation therapy after consolidation
Supportive care: analgesia, blood pressure control, nutritional support

t.b: Promotes differentiation of residual tumour cells; given after intensive chemotherapy
Controls catecholamine‑induced hypertension; avoid β‑blocker alone

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance detects relapse and late effects of therapy.
b: Clinical exam and abdominal ultrasound every 3 months for 2 years
Urine catecholamines annually for 5 years
Audiology, cardiac echo and endocrine assessment after intensive therapy

sections.p: Other small‑round‑blue‑cell tumours can mimic neuroblastoma on imaging and histology.
b: Wilms tumour – kidney origin, usually older children
Ewing sarcoma – peripheral bone lesion, CD99 positive
Rhabdomyosarcoma – striated‑muscle differentiation

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal, leading to delayed diagnosis.
b: Urine catecholamines can be normal in well‑differentiated ganglioneuroma
MIBG scan negative in non‑avid tumours; consider FDG‑PET

faq.a: Amplification predicts aggressive behaviour and places the patient in the high‑risk group, dictating intensive therapy.
Yes, especially stage MS disease in infants; careful observation is an accepted approach for low‑risk cases.

faq.q: What is the significance of opsoclonus‑myoclonus?
faq.a: It is a paraneoplastic syndrome indicating neuroblastoma; its presence should prompt tumour search even without a palpable mass.

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect neuroblastoma in a toddler with an abdominal mass? — Palpable firm, non‑tender mass, hypertension, and possible opsoclonus‑myoclonus.
How does the INRG staging system differ from the older INSS system? — INRG uses imaging‑defined risk factors and does not require surgical resection for stage assignment.
A child presents with fever, bone pain and a normal abdominal ultrasound. Which test should you order next and why? — Urine VMA/HVA to detect catecholamine secretion, guiding further imaging.

Why is cyclophosphamide preferred over high‑dose methotrexate in initial neuroblastoma chemotherapy in low‑resource settings? — Cyclophosphamide requires less intensive monitoring and hydration, making it safer where supportive care is limited.

What are the key features that distinguish neuroblastoma from Wilms tumour on imaging? — Neuroblastoma arises from adrenal or paraspinal locations, often crosses midline; Wilms tumour is confined to the kidney and displaces rather than infiltrates.

Explain why β‑blocker monotherapy is avoided in neuroblastoma‑related hypertension. — Catecholamine excess causes α‑mediated vasoconstriction; blocking β receptors alone can precipitate unopposed α activity and worsen hypertension.

A patient with stage 4 neuroblastoma has normal urine catecholamines. How do you proceed? — Proceed with imaging (CT/MRI) and biopsy because non‑secreting tumours exist; staging cannot rely on catecholamines alone.

What long‑term complication should you monitor after high‑dose chemotherapy and stem‑cell rescue? — Secondary malignancies, cardiac dysfunction, and growth/endocrine disturbances; regular follow‑up is essential.
